a104.titolo: Facebook is giving users more control over their algorithm
a104.testo: Facebook is the latest social media platform to give users greater control over the algorithm that determines what appears in their feeds. Meta announced the launch of its new AI-powered feature, “Your Algorithm,” on Tuesday, a feature it first launched on Instagram. The new tool allows Facebook users to influence the content they see in Feed and Reels by describing their preferences in their own words using natural language. Rather than relying entirely on automated recommendations, users can now communicate directly with the platform about the topics and content they want to see more or less frequently. According to Meta, the feature is designed to make content recommendations more relevant. Users can adjust their preferences and interact with the algorithms responsible for ranking and recommending posts, with changes reflected in their recommendations in real time. The company has also updated Facebook’s three-dot menu, making it easier for users to manage their content preferences directly from individual posts. By opening the menu, users can access “Your Algorithm” or select the “Interested” and “Not interested” options to indicate whether particular content aligns with their preferences. Meta says the platform may ask follow-up questions to better understand what users liked or disliked, allowing them to provide more detailed feedback. Users can explain what they want to see more or less of, helping Facebook refine its recommendations based on their responses. The introduction of “Your Algorithm” reflects Meta’s broader effort to give people more influence over their social media experiences as AI increasingly shapes content discovery. The move signals a shift away from the traditional recommendation systems that have shaped social media experiences for years, br…

a107.titolo: Google Play now lets anyone build private, vibe-coded apps that run on Android
a107.testo: Your vibe-coded applications can now be easily run on Android smartphones without having to first go public on the Google Play Store, the tech giant announced on Tuesday. A new feature will allow users to launch their own personal apps on their device via Google Play using their standard Google account, but they will remain completely private. These personal apps won’t show up in Google Play’s search or listing pages, and won’t be shared with anyone except for the app’s creator. The idea comes as more people are experimenting with building their own applications via AI for specific, personal needs. However, being able to use that app on their own Android device has meant publishing to Google Play, making it accessible to the Play Store’s some 3 billion users. That led many to limit their vibe-coding efforts to web apps that could run on any device instead of something built natively for Android. Now, Google says Android device owners can vibe-code an app using Google AI Studio, then launch it for their own use. These apps are still required to comply with Google Play’s existing policies but allow users to experiment more directly with building apps for Android. Initially, the feature will be available to users in the U.S., age 18 and up. “That’s why the future of apps on Google Play is personal, secure, and built by everyone — and it’s why Play is leading the charge and moving from ‘there’s an app for that’ to ‘there’s an app for me,’” said Sam Bright, Google’s VP and GM for the Google Play and Developer Ecosystem, in a press briefing ahead of Tuesday’s launch. “We started Google Play with a simple goal: to connect you with the apps you love. But after today, we hope it’s clear: Play has evolved to become so much more than that.” In the months ahead, the company said t…

a93.titolo: Google makes it easier to launch your vibe-coded apps
a93.testo: The next time you vibe-code a custom app with Google’s AI Studio, you won’t have to connect your phone to a computer to install it. On Tuesday, Google announced a new feature in the US that will allow you to launch personal apps directly through the Play Store. Google makes it easier to launch your vibe-coded apps You can now launch your vibe-coded app directly from the Google Play Store. Google first launched the ability to vibe-code personal Android apps in May. Even though you can now launch your custom apps in Google Play, the company notes it will continue to keep them “secure, private, and separate from the public store catalog.” You can also launch them using a standard Google account, and the company will soon add the ability to share your app with a select group of people, too. Though this might make it easier to play around with experimental apps, Google is positioning it as an on-ramp of sorts for fledgling developers. “If you want to share your app with the world, Google Play helps you graduate to a professional developer account with the same Trust & Safety reviews and high-quality standards as professional developers,” Sam Bright, Google’s vice president and general manager of Google Play, writes in the announcement.

u1a104.titolo: Anthropic’s self-replicating AI warning is alarming deja vu
u1a104.testo: Are legions of smart devices — fridges, ovens, vacuum cleaners, lawnmowers, security cameras, and TVs — conspiring to take over the internet? No. But they could soon be unwitting hosts to self-replicating AI models that spread from device to device and prove remarkably difficult to contain. Anthropic’s self-replicating AI warning is alarming deja vu Anthropic says its research found ‘signs of life for AI worms,’ that could colonize household devices. Experts say they have a point. Welcome to the unsettling world of AI worms, where, depending on who you ask, the prospect of models spreading uncontrollably across household appliances is either an imminent cybersecurity risk or another case of AI companies spreading doomer-tinged hype. In a blog post published this week, Anthropic warns that small AI models could be “months away” from acquiring such capabilities. Its experiments offer some evidence to support that, but leave a huge gap between what researchers have demonstrated and the looming threat they foretell. Still, experts who spoke to The Verge say that while computer worms and fears of self-replicating AI are nothing new, recent advances suggest there are good reasons to take the warnings seriously. Self-replicating machines have long haunted AI safety researchers. They raise the prospect of systems spreading beyond human control that are difficult, if not impossible, to shut down. As with many fears about advancing AI, attention has largely focused on increasingly powerful frontier models, such as OpenAI’s Astra or Anthropic’s Mythos. But a key limiting factor is their size: They are colossal. Potentially containing trillions of parameters — values learned during training — frontier models require vast computing resources, largely confining them to data centers,…

u1a148.titolo: Se l’AI impara a replicarsi: codici malevoli autonomi potrebbero invadere elettrodomestici e Tv
u1a148.testo: Se l’AI impara a replicarsi: codici malevoli autonomi potrebbero invadere elettrodomestici e Tv Il lavoro di Anthropic sull’autoreplicazione dei modelli AI affronta una questione concreta: in quali condizioni un sistema potrebbe sfruttare le risorse informatiche disponibili per creare copie di sé stesso, L’ipotesi che un sistema di intelligenza artificiale possa replicarsi autonomamente non appartiene più a copioni di film di fantascienza, ma potrebbe essere realtà a breve. Il lavoro di Anthropic sull’autoreplicazione dei modelli AI affronta una questione concreta: in quali condizioni un sistema potrebbe sfruttare le risorse informatiche disponibili per creare copie di sé stesso, trasferirle su altre macchine e continuare a operare senza dipendere da un’infrastruttura controllata direttamente dai suoi sviluppatori? Chiedilo al Sole Il tema rappresenta una priorità per chi si occupa di cybersecurity e protezione delle infrastrutture critiche, perché delinea uno scenario di rischio concreto: agenti AI capaci di adattarsi a dispositivi diversi, sfruttare sistemi vulnerabili e propagarsi attraverso reti connesse, riducendo progressivamente la necessità di intervento umano. Gli esperimenti non dimostrano che esista già una minaccia di questo tipo operativa su larga scala, ma mostrano che alcune delle barriere tecniche stanno diventando meno solide. Per chi difende reti e infrastrutture, il rischio non è soltanto teorico: è la possibilità che malware potenziati dall’AI trasformino migliaia di dispositivi IoT compromessi in una rete distribuita, capace di espandersi e adattare le proprie operazioni con una velocità e una flessibilità difficili da contrastare. u1a100.titolo: OpenAI claims an ex-employee took its product plans and presented them to Apple
u1a100.testo: OpenAI claims a former employee took more than 100 files related to its product plans before joining Apple. In a document filed on Wednesday, OpenAI accuses the unnamed employee of sending this information to a personal account and then presenting it to Apple leadership, including the vice president of the company’s operations in Asia. OpenAI claims an ex-employee took its product plans and presented them to Apple The former employee took more than 100 confidential files before leaving to join Apple, OpenAI alleges. The filing, reported earlier by Reuters, is tied to a legal battle between Apple and OpenAI over trade secrets — but this time, OpenAI is doing the accusing. It alleges that the files in question contain images of at least one unreleased device, along with supplier information, engineering data, project files, standards for cosmetic finishes, and reports about the “coating and sealing of hardware components.” OpenAI also links Apple’s new HomeView smart display and the range of other devices it revealed this week to the former employee’s presentation. “That presentation appears to have happened months ago — and now, armed with that information, Apple is making a new push into AI-enabled products,” OpenAI claims, while citing an article and a company announcement about Apple’s new product releases. Apple’s product plans typically operate on a very long timeline, and its smart display has been rumored for years. Conversely, Apple accuses OpenAI of stealing confidential documents and spying on hardware prototypes to help build its own products. “OpenAI is very concerned that its trade secret and confidential information is now circulating inside Apple, where Apple engineers can shape Apple’s upcoming products based on OpenAI’s confidential and innovative work,…

u1a122.titolo: Recording device hidden in toilet paper found in top-secret OpenAI meeting room
u1a122.testo: It took OpenAI two days to notice that a recording device was hidden in a restricted executive conference room where leadership met to discuss highly confidential information, including technical progress, government engagements, and commercial partnerships. Only those with special clearance are supposed to access that room. But the FBI believes the recording device was planted by Abdulrahman Alfozan, a 35-year-old engineer from Saudi Arabia, who became a permanent US legal resident in 2020. In a press release Tuesday announcing his arrest, the FBI alleged that chatbot logs and CCTV footage suggested that Alfozan—who worked as an OpenAI engineer for more than a year—sought to use the device to spy on OpenAI and risked leaking trade secrets in a way that threatened national security. To conceal the USB device, Alfozan allegedly wrapped it in toilet paper, then plugged it into the back of a conference room television. The device was likely planted on September 28, and OpenAI found it on September 30 and quickly determined that its contents were encrypted, the FBI said. Days later, on October 5, OpenAI installed a camera in that conference room, and the CCTV footage allegedly showed Alfozan attempting to retrieve the recording device that same day. If convicted of violating laws against unlawful recordings, Alfozan faces up to five years in prison and a $250,000 fine, the FBI said. OpenAI did not immediately move to eject Alfozan as a suspected spy. Instead, it gradually cut off his access to systems while working with the FBI to analyze the recording device’s contents. Once enough evidence was gathered, OpenAI timed Alfozan’s firing on Friday with the FBI’s arrest.

u1a123.titolo: Anthropic warns small AI models could self-replicate through IoT devices
u1a123.testo: AI company Anthropic is warning that advances in small AI models could soon usher in a new era of self-replicating malware that’s capable of infecting smart fridges, vacuum cleaners, and a wide range of other Internet-of-things devices and is more resistant to takedown. By next year, smaller AI models may be able to autonomously self-replicate on all kinds of IoT devices, the company said. Eventually, the capability could enable computer worms, which propagate without requiring human interaction and are capable of infecting unfamiliar IoT devices. An experiment the company performed recently revealed significant challenges in bringing such an AI malware replicator to fruition, so the finding is necessarily tempered. Still, the results do raise concerns about the possibility of new forms of computer worms. Challenging to shut down Anthropic further warned not only about the new potential malware, but also that it could be difficult to stop. In its blog post, it wrote that “a replicator like this would be challenging to shut down, since there’s no centralized point to shut off—though it may be slow (with a doubling time of days). Unlike non-AI malware, it could also figure out unfamiliar devices on its own.” Smaller AI models require much less powerful hardware to run than do frontier models. Anthropic ran small open-weight models on real or simulated low-cost, off-brand Android TV boxes and other types of IoT hardware. Company researchers found that by using quantization to represent the models using fewer bits and splitting the workloads into “shards” running on each device, the models were able to establish inference, meaning that the model weights loaded and could generate output. The lightweight Gemma4-26B-A4B model required just 15 boxes, each equipped with only 4G…

u1a153.titolo: Il sofisticato dispositivo che spiava OpenAI costa 13,99 dollari
u1a153.testo: La notizia del giorno è l’operazione di spionaggio sventata negli uffici di OpenAI. La casa madre di ChatGPT ha scoperto un sofisticato dispositivo di registrazione nascosto all’interno di uno dei suoi uffici nella sede di San Francisco, collegato a una porta USB dietro a un televisore. È stato individuato anche il responsabile, un ex dipendente già preso in consegna dall’FBI e che ora rischia grosso. Qual è l’artefatto dell’ingegneria impiegato, forse, per rubare i segreti di Sam Altman e soci? Un modulo da 13,99 dollari. Questa è la microspia messa negli uffici di OpenAI È quanto si capisce dalle immagini pubblicate dal Dipartimento di Giustizia statunitense (nonostante la risoluzione infima). Si vede chiaramente il marchio del produttore, Seeed Studio. Il modello preciso sembra essere lo XIAO ESP32-S3 Sense, che chiunque può acquistare dal suo store online. Integra un microfono e una fotocamera da 2 megapixel, racchiusi in dimensioni piuttosto compatte (21x15x17,8 millimetri). Ha poi in dotazione un modulo Wi-Fi in grado di trasmettere informazioni ed è proprio attraverso questo componente che Abdulrahman Alfozan, il responsabile dell’azione, potrebbe aver rubato informazioni riservate a OpenAI. Curiosamente, Seeed Studio ha condiviso nei mesi scorsi un video che spiega come trasformarlo in un dispositivo di intelligenza artificiale, qualcosa di simile al fallimentare Humane AI Pin. Un’altra immagine condivisa dal Dipartimento di Giustizia è quella che ritrae Alfozan in una sorta di selfie catturato il 5 ottobre dall’apparecchio (quando era già stato scoperto, ma non ancora rimosso).
